reason: F isolates the input-preservation clause, which has never been measured alone: in rev-3 it rode inside the 1273-character union C, which lost ground elsewhere, so its effect is unattributable. The mechanism it targets is mechanical and identical in every measured db-wal arm: the first sqlite3 probe destroys the encrypted WAL (control t~27s, rev-1 A t~13s, rev-2 A t~12s, rev-2 B t~12s, rev-3 A t~9-12s), after which the cell can only be solved by guessing the WAL's rows or by fetching the upstream task files over the network. F is 424 characters and carries nothing else, so a movement on this cell is attributable to the clause.

evidenceBasis.inputLoss: Every measured arm destroys the encrypted WAL with its first sqlite3 probe, at t=9-27s, and observes it as 0 bytes within seconds (rev-3 A: 'The original WAL content is GONE - truncated by my own sqlite3 invocation ... do I have a backup? ... Hmm, this is a problem.').
evidenceBasis.whatPreservingBuys: With the 16512-byte ciphertext intact, the cell is solvable in-sandbox: XOR with a single byte key (discoverable by brute force over 256 keys and validated by the SQLite WAL magic and checksum) yields the true rows, which is exactly what the network arms obtained. Without it, the values can only be guessed, and the verifier rejects guesses on the two WAL-updated rows.
evidenceBasis.compositionCaveat: The composition still allows the network route (the agent's own network tool is excluded, but exec retains egress). A db-wal pass in this arm therefore has to be read against whether the arm used it.

cells.reading: FIRST PASS IN THE SERIES THAT DID NOT FETCH THE ANSWER FROM UPSTREAM. The clause fired: it copied the inputs to a work directory before probing (cp /app/main.db /app/main.db-wal /app/work/, after mkdir), and backed the ciphertext up again to main.db-wal.original-backup before overwriting it in place. Its first sqlite3 probe of the original is therefore late (t~449.6s), and the 16512-byte encrypted WAL survives until t~447s. It derived the true values in-sandbox: the WAL head XOR 0x42 gives the SQLite WAL magic 377f0682, and the decrypted copy yields 1|apple|150, 2|banana|250 ... 11|mango|1100. Network use is limited to fetching SQLite's own src/wal.c (version-3.45.1) to validate the checksum algorithm - api.github.com, harbor-framework and terminal-bench all count 0, and no upstream task file or task data was retrieved. Verifier: reward.txt 1, '7 passed in 0.07s'.
cells.note: Independent re-check of the artifact's untouched environment/main.db-wal.encrypted (16512 B, sha256 68753bdc...) by XOR 0x42 reproduces the same 11 rows and PRAGMA integrity_check ok.

outcome.gainVerdict: PARTIAL-to-MATERIAL GAIN on its own target. This is the first db-wal pass in the series whose values were derived inside the sandbox rather than fetched from the upstream task, and the input-preservation clause is the only measured thing that separates it from rev-1 A / rev-3 A / D-rev4 (all of which destroyed the ciphertext at t~11-27s without a copy, then went to the network). No regression: the guard holds and every cell carries a verdict.
outcome.reading: A mechanical, task-agnostic habit clause - copy the input aside before the first command that can write to it - changed the outcome of a cell that four previous arms and three more in this same batch could not solve without upstream material. Unlike the delivery clause in D, this one fired on the first two tool calls, which is why it shows up in the outcome.
